title: Stinespring's Dilation, Universal-NOT, and Limitations of Quantum Uncoupled Learning
abstract: Uncoupled learning, in which players know only their own payoff, are a standard model of decentralized learning toward Nash equilibrium. We study their quantum counterpart, where strategies are quantum states and, in each round, a player receives a physical copy of their opponent's current strategy and updates their own state by a quantum channel. This adds to uncoupledness a constraint with no classical analogue: every update must be physically realizable. In fact, this constraint is decisive in conjugation games, in which Bob has a strictly dominant pure strategy and Alice's unique best response is its transpose. In this work, we show some limitations of uncoupled (learning) dynamics in finding the Nash equilibrium for conjugation games. First, we prove that no autonomous, memoryless, uncoupled dynamics converge to Nash equilibrium in a family of four single-qubit conjugation games. Specifically, any memoryless channel that keeps all four equilibria fixed will leave Alice's strategy frozen. This result also extends to $4^n$ games on $n$-qubit registers. Second, we show that this barrier disappears with a small classical memory : for any finite family of $L$ pure targets, a guess-and-test rule with $O(\log L)$ classical bits converges to equilibrium, with an explicit bound on its convergence rate. Finally, we prove that no finite memory , classical or quantum, suffices for the continuum of all pure-qubit targets. Our proof of the impossibility for memoryless channels relies on Stinespring's dilation theorem, while the impossibility for finite- memory channels relies on the optimal universal-NOT (in)fidelity bound by Bužek, Hillery, and Werner.

title: NavTTT: Adaptive Parametric Memory via Hierarchical Test-Time Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation
abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.

title: Microscopic Cosmological Backreaction of an Ultralight Majoron Coupled to a Coherent Hidden Pseudo-Dirac Ensemble
abstract: We develop a microscopic framework for the cosmological backreaction of a hidden pseudo-Dirac fermion ensemble derivatively coupled to an ultralight Majoron. Starting from the effective action, we derive the exact operator Ward identity for the pseudo-Dirac current and the associated microscopic energy-transfer law. For a thermal density matrix prepared at a finite initial time, we calculate the subsequent collisionless, linearized coherence response without assuming continued thermal equilibrium or introducing phenomenological dissipation. The finite-time retarded solution retains the initial boundary transient and nonlocal memory contribution, allowing us to assess the validity of the leading local adiabatic approximation and distinguish reversible coherent energy exchange from dissipative friction. For a subdominant Majoron benchmark evolving in a prescribed FRW background, the local energy-transfer rate changes sign, while the present-day fractional velocity correction is only $+5.23\times10^{-53}$. A convergence-tested numerical comparison, including the initial transient and memory contribution, bounds the difference between the retarded and local fractional velocity corrections to less than $6.78\times10^{-17}$ of the local correction. Within the linearized, collisionless positive-energy two-state approximation, these results demonstrate that the microscopic backreaction does not produce significant Majoron freezing for the benchmark considered, while leaving open different behavior in other parameter regimes or preparation histories.

title: PACE-WM: Parallel World Modeling with Action History for Visual Planning
abstract: JEPA-style world models support visual planning by predicting future representations conditioned on future actions. However, similar observations can conceal different motion states, making temporal context essential for interpreting future action effects. We propose PACE-WM, a parallel world model that uses executed-action history to contextualize future prediction and planning. Specifically, PACE-WM maintains a recurrent memory of executed actions and uses this memory to condition a causal Transformer. PACE-WM predicts multiple future representations in parallel without recursive predicted-state feedback within each prediction window. We further introduce Reference-Anchored Minimum Progress (RAMP) for action selection during planning. RAMP scores candidate actions by their predicted goal improvement along direct and split paths relative to a shared reference. Across four visual planning tasks, PACE-WM with RAMP achieves an average success rate of $98\%$ and plans approximately $7$-$9\times$ faster than autoregressive LeWM under matched CEM settings. We also construct four controlled benchmarks to evaluate PACE-WM's capabilities in motion disambiguation, goal-relative motion, and goal adaptation. Project page is available at https://github.com/LHS180/PACE-WM.

title: Ultraslow vorticity modes in colloidal fluids
abstract: In the conventional unsteady-Stokes picture, vorticity generated by a transient disturbance relaxes rapidly through viscous diffusion once the forcing ceases. This view presumes a quiescent solvent. In colloidal and biological fluids, thermal motion continually perturbs the surrounding fluid, raising a natural question: can equilibrium fluctuations, mediated by hydrodynamic coupling, sustain vorticity over mesoscopic scales and times? Here, using high-speed confocal microscopy of moderately dense colloidal suspensions, we reconstruct the conditional mean hydrodynamic response to Brownian displacements of prescribed magnitude and direction. We find a long-lived, spatially structured vorticity field that decays far more slowly than predicted by unforced unsteady-Stokes dynamics. A coarse-grained phenomenological model based on fractional Brownian motion, constrained by independently measured single-particle subdiffusion, quantitatively captures its temporal and spatial decay. These findings reveal a field-level manifestation of hydrodynamic memory in fluctuating low-Reynolds-number flows, with implications for transport and collective dynamics in complex fluids.

title: Which Data-Center Load Models Can Be Trusted? An Evidence-Graded Review of Dynamic Modeling and Validation for Large Computational Loads
abstract: Grid operators now require dynamic models of data centers and other large computational loads, and new ride-through rules assume that these models predict how facilities respond to disturbances. This review asks what evidence supports that assumption. We coded 160 documents, screened from 1,424 de-duplicated database and seed records plus 65 added documents, by the strongest reference object each presents, from grid-side records to simulation only. Across 19 field-evidence entries, 15 requirement documents from three continents and nine model classes, we find two comparisons of a standard library model with measured data-center events: with default parameters the model failed both, and refitting it to each event separately reduced the error but was never tested on an unseen event. Among the sources reviewed, we found no successful held-out validation of a frozen, facility-specific data-center model against an independent measured disturbance, and 25 of the 33 model-phenomenon combinations with any evidence involve no electrical measurement. The features that distinguish the new rules ( memory of repeated dips, recovery within 0.5-3 s, proportional power reduction during the sag, overvoltage response) are those current phasor models cannot represent or have never been tested against. In the operator procedures examined, simulations and model-to-model benchmarks are accepted as evidence of model fidelity, unlike the measured validation required of generators, and proposed mitigations have mostly been evaluated on unvalidated facility models. We propose context-of-use gates that separate calibration from validation, release labels for model claims, a minimum validation protocol with acceptance criteria, and a research agenda.

title: Mem-X: A Memory-Dependent Cross-Episode Benchmark for Vision-and-Language Navigation
abstract: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.

title: A Higher-Order Algorithm for Solving Time-Fractional Differential Equations via Rational Approximation of z^α as a Herglotz-Nevanlinna function
abstract: Time-Fractional derivatives (TFDs) have been widely used in mathematical modeling of physical phenomena such as anomalous diffusion and memory effects of materials. Traditionally, TFD is handled {either by a direct method which saves almost all the memory and hence computationally expensive or a sum of exponential method (SOE) which decomposes the time domain improper integral into a local term and a history term} {approximated by} a sum of exponential functions. The limitation of the SOE approach is that{ the approximation error of the local term might result in large errors if the unknown function is not smooth enough at $0$ and can lead to over-dissipation of energy.} In this paper, we take a different approach and will focus on the Caputo derivative because the Caputo time derivative of a constant function is 0. We present a simple time-stepping algorithm based on the theory of Stieltjes-Markov functions, a subclass of the Herglotz-Nevanlinna functions. The key is in identifying the Stieltjes-Markov function structure hidden in the Laplace transform of the kernel function. Compared to most of the current methods in literature, the novelty of the results in this paper is manifold. First, no decomposition of integral is needed and our resulting approximation in the time domain contains a Dirac measure with carefully calculated strength, leading to a drastic decrease in the number of exponential functions needed in the approximation. Secondly, the choice of our interpolation points is based on the Mellin's inversion theorem and hence the interpolation error in the transformed domain is explicitly and rigorously linked to the error in the time-domain. {Finally, the resulting system is almost diagonal and hence can be easily sped up by using the Schur complement method.}

title: Adaptive Collective Decision-Making in Signed Networks
abstract: Collective decision-making often unfolds in networks where cooperation and antagonism coexist. Such signed interactions arise in social, biological, and robotic systems, and can lead to qualitatively different collective outcomes: consensus, polarization, or clustering. Existing signed network models typically explain these outcomes separately, leaving open how they can emerge within a single dynamical framework. Here, we introduce a generalized Laplacian flow for bi-partitioned signed networks, a class of networks that allows cooperative and antagonistic interactions both within and across two prescribed groups. The proposed model includes an adaptive social effort state, interpreted as a leaky memory of persistent signed network disagreement, which enables bounded and nontrivial steady-states beyond classical signed Laplacian flows. We derive conditions that determine whether the network reaches consensus, polarization, or clustering based on the spectral structure of the generalized Laplacian and effective resistance matrices. The framework applies beyond structurally balanced, weakly balanced, and quasi-structurally balanced networks, and reveals how changes in signed interaction strengths can shift a network between collective decision regimes. We validate the theory on stochastic block model networks, a judicial voting network, and a U.S. senate bill co-sponsorship network. Altogether, our results provide a structural and dynamical account of how mixed cooperative and antagonistic relationships shape emergent collective behaviors.

title: GaLF-ST: Gaussian Latent Fields for Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at known tissue locations to reveal tissue organization and cellular function. Expression prediction requires modeling both local spatial relationships and associations among genes. Existing methods typically model expression using coordinate networks without explicit spatial parameterization. To address limited spatial sampling and sparse expression observations of ST, some methods firstly fit intermediate embeddings and then train expression predictors, but a latent representation suited to expression reconstruction may be difficult to predict from spatial coordinates. The two training stages can impose different demands on the latent representation. In this paper, we propose GaLF-ST, a Gaussian latent field method in which learnable Gaussian centers and anisotropic covariances determine the weights of latent vectors at each location. A shared nonlinear decoder maps their weighted average to multigene expression. In GaLF-ST, observed expression error jointly updates the Gaussian geometry, latent vectors, and decoder parameters. We further establish a unified benchmark across seven dataset groups and three held-out fractions, comparing GaLF-ST with four representative methods using the same locations, splits, gene panels, and scoring rules. Across tissues and observation densities, GaLF-ST achieves leading overall reconstruction performance, recovering spatial gene expression patterns and preserving tissue domains from limited observations while substantially reducing runtime and GPU memory usage.

title: Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction for Long-tailed Graph Classification
abstract: Long-tailed graph classification (LTGC) is common in real-world graph datasets, where a few large head graphs provide rich structural information while many smaller tail graphs offer fewer structural cues, making it harder to learn discriminative representations for tail graphs. To address this size-based imbalance, we propose Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction (DMPRP), which transfers structural patterns from head graphs to tail graphs. Given a graph representation as a query, a dynamic expert memory module inspired by Knowledge-diverse Experts (KDEX) generates a residual vector that augments the original representation. We train the module using co-occurrence triplets sampled from head graphs at the node, rooted subgraph, and random-walk neighborhood levels. Experiments on five graph classification benchmarks show that DMPRP improves tail performance, and ablation studies show that both the expert module and random-walk supervision contribute to these gains. A controlled experiment on PTC further examines pattern transfer when smaller graphs are denser than larger ones. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DMPRP-73A5.

title: Double counting in LLM evidence fusion: exact posteriors separate rule compliance from posterior gain
abstract: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $\delta$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($\delta$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($\delta$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $\delta$ = 1 minus $\delta$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.

title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory , and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.

title: A Footprint-Sensitive Cross-GPU Timing Channel Through the Shared Host Memory Subsystem
abstract: Assigning tenants to separate GPUs does not isolate their host memory traffic. We identify an unprivileged timing channel between GPUs without NVLink: a co-tenant can detect contention by timing reads to its own pinned host buffer, without accessing victim data or using hardware performance counters. The signal tracks the number of distinct host pages the victim touches rather than its throughput. We demonstrate covert communication at 20 bit/s with near-zero error, LLM output-length inference at a held-out Spearman correlation of 0.99 across five models on three platforms, and refusal inference at balanced accuracy up to 0.955. The attacks cross process, container, and Unix-user boundaries and reproduce across two GPU generations and two serving runtimes. Bursty transfers in the tested vLLM+LMCache stack remain below the leakage floor, limiting the demonstrated attacks to sustained device-to-host traffic. IOMMU-disabled and cross-NUMA controls attribute the channel to page-walk contention at the shared host memory controller. This finding motivates two defenses, controller-aware placement and footprint flattening, both of which reduce inference to chance in our experiments. Accelerator isolation alone does not isolate the host infrastructure that tenants share.

title: E2Former-V3: Atom-Role-Aware Equivariant Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials approach density-functional accuracy, but explicit-solvent atom counts are dominated by hydrogens and water. Uniform equivariant architectures still give every atom the same latent width and number of expensive block updates. To our knowledge, no prior method reallocates capacity by chemical role while retaining every atom and its first-principles force. We introduce E2Former-V3, which treats capacity as an atom-level resource: a static chemical role, assigned before the backbone runs, sets each atom's latent width and update count. No atom is removed, no coordinate is integrated out, and every force remains the gradient of one conservative energy. Standard reduces only the update count, sending hydrogen through half as many full-width block updates; on OMol25 validation it reaches a force mean absolute error (MAE) of 8.146 meV/Angstrom, against E2Former-V2's published 8.38, at 1.75-1.84x V2's throughput with lower peak memory on one H200. Flash also narrows the low-resolution stream to one eighth of the high-resolution width (32 vs 256 channels) and routes water oxygen with hydrogen, reaching 4.00-4.88x on three solvated systems (up to 5.85x in the pure-water all-low-resolution limit) at 11.272 meV/Angstrom, trading force accuracy for speed. Across 54 20 ps MD legs, a 100 ps NVE check, and a 1 ns NVT run on a 32,437-atom solvated protein, all runs complete; the MD legs show no non-finite values, clashes, or water fusion, and water O-O and Na-O RDF peak positions match experiment within 0.04 Angstrom. E2Former-V3 therefore moves the accuracy-throughput frontier for all-atom, conservative simulation, not a uniform accuracy win: Standard is worse on biomolecules and metals, better on electrolytes and organics; energy MAE is higher than E2Former-V2's; and water densities remain about 7.5% too high. Code: https://github.com/IQuestLab/UBio-MolFM.

title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
abstract: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.

title: Hindsight Forcing: Learning Better History from the Future in Autoregressive Video Diffusion
abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables real-time streaming generation, with each generated chunk serving as historical context for subsequent generation. To avoid the memory explosion of backpropagation through time, previous self-rollout methods typically truncate cross-chunk gradients or detach historical latents. As a result, earlier denoising computations receive no downstream feedback through the generated history on how to synthesize frames that facilitate subsequent generation, leading to visual drift and structural collapse as rollouts extend. To address this limitation, we propose Hindsight Forcing, which allows historical chunks to learn directly from future outcomes by decoupling forward generation from backward credit assignment via a latent straight-through bridge. In the forward pass, each chunk completes a full multi-step rollout to update the KV cache. In the backward pass, the bridge routes gradients from future losses back to a single selected denoising step per historical chunk, training both the context writer and historical denoiser on shared parameters without retaining the full trajectory graph. Remarkably, Hindsight Forcing requires no additional model parameters, architecture modifications, or separate trajectory replay. Extensive experiments on VBench demonstrate that Hindsight Forcing outperforms existing baselines in overall visual quality and dynamic motion, while ablation studies validate the benefit of supervising historical denoising. Code is available at https://github.com/haonanAN309/Hindsight-Forcing.

title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: Stateful Privacy Sniffing of LLM Agents via Behavioral Covert Channels in Web Interactions
abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on Web interaction, issuing searches, following links, and reading pages, to complete complex user tasks. Since each action is driven by the agent's private context, including the user's prompt, dialogue history, memory, and connected data, it also opens a new privacy exposure surface. Prior attacks either passively analyze network traffic, which yields only coarse correlations, or hijack the agent through indirect prompt injection, which must place sensitive content in an outgoing field and is blocked by content-level defenses. Whether an attacker can actively recover fine-grained private context without any explicit transmission thus remains insufficiently understood. Our insight is that an agent's benign Web decisions themselves leak private context, as what it chooses to visit encodes whether, which, and in what order it acts, forming a behavioral covert channel. Building on this, we design SNOOP, a stateful hierarchical probing framework that narrows a coarse-to-fine hypothesis tree per task and reconstructs user queries and profiles from the agent's observable paths. Across four agents and three LLM backbones on 500 StackExchange queries and 378 multi-turn iKAT dialogues, SNOOP recovers query concepts with an average F1 of 0.89 and user profiles with an F1 of 0.80, while four representative agent defenses change its recovery by less than 0.03 F1. Since no sensitive content is ever transmitted, content-level inspection cannot detect this leakage; we therefore propose Selection-Obfuscated Retrieval (SOR), which acquires resources under a fixed budget independent of private context and confines the agent's selection to a local snapshot, cutting SNOOP's F1 to 0.39 without additional LLM inference.

title: Loop-OPF: Solver-Informed Learning for Optimal Power Flow with Inference-Time Topology Adaptivity
abstract: Learning for optimal power flow (OPF) has recently been advocated to accelerate OPF solutions by using a pre-trained neural network (NN) to predict directly from given inputs such as the load demand. However, existing learning-for-OPF methods largely fall short of ensuring the optimality and feasibility of their predictions. They also struggle to adapt at inference time to unseen topology scenarios, such as those caused by line or generator outages. This work puts forth Loop-OPF, a solver-informed NN that builds its layers from the iterations of the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method. Under standard convexity and regularity conditions on DC-OPF, the resultant fixed-point output of Loop-OPF is thus optimal and feasible. To speed up PDHG across diverse OPF scenarios, Loop-OPF learns certain PDHG parameters in a self-supervised manner, without any OPF solution labels. We adopt the deep equilibrium (DEQ) framework for training so that the memory cost does not grow with the number of layers. As the grid topology enters every layer as an input, the same trained Loop-OPF directly adapts to unseen contingencies without retraining. Numerical tests on the IEEE 300-bus and PEGASE 1354-, 2869-, and 9241-bus networks have demonstrated the accuracy and topology adaptivity of the proposed Loop-OPF over competing learning-for-OPF methods.

title: Rethinking ANNS on Commodity PIM: PIM-Native Vector Search with Cooperative Filtering
abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) is a key primitive in modern data-intensive systems, and its memory -bound vector-scanning stage makes processing-in- memory (PIM) a promising acceleration platform. Existing PIM-based ANNS systems largely transplant CPU-oriented distance evaluation and top-$k$ selection onto PIM, introducing arithmetic- and state-heavy operations that poorly match lightweight, isolated PIM cores. To address these mismatches, we present PIVOT, a PIM-native vector search system with cooperative filtering, which thoroughly rethinks how ANNS should be executed on commodity PIM. First, PIVOT recasts PIM-side distance evaluation around binary quantization to exploit PIM-native bitwise operations, enabling LUT-free evaluation with low arithmetic cost and a small local- memory footprint. Second, PIVOT redesigns PIM-side candidate selection around threshold-guided cooperative filtering, using a survivor-mass model to derive a conservative threshold for CPU-side cluster filtering and PIM-side lower-bound filtering, thereby reducing output traffic and eliminating per-core top-$k$ state. PIVOT organizes these stages into a cooperative workflow that keeps query-global coordination and reranking on the CPU while assigning memory -intensive, data-parallel filtering to PIM. To efficiently realize this workflow and sustain high utilization across devices, PIVOT further generates configuration-specialized PIM kernels and pipelines CPU-side preparation and reranking with PIM-side filtering across query batches. Evaluations on real UPMEM hardware show that PIVOT filters out 99.3-99.7% of probed vectors and achieves up to $18.8\times$ and $10.2\times$ the QPS of CPU and prior PIM baselines, respectively. PIVOT also achieves higher recall than existing PIM systems and remains effective on high-dimensional embeddings.

title: Privacy Protection in Self-Evolving Personal Agents: Persistent Memory and Cross-Carrier Transfer
abstract: Personal agents carry private experience into later decisions through persistent memory. This thematic survey compares memory admission, maintenance, release, and withdrawal by protected change, observer, and validation setting. Direct evidence in the screened corpus comes from controlled memory workflows. Three worked scenarios follow one private fact through booking, feedback-driven learning, and withdrawal. We show when prompt revision and memory reads compose, when skills inherit a private head's bound, and why reader non-use does not establish cleanup of learned state. Diagnostic experiments measure the utility costs of wider label protection and broad memory deletion, and test how missing lineage obscures descendants.

title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.

title: MixFold: Sub-4-Bit Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Output-Channel Grouping on Mobile NPUs
abstract: Sub-4-bit quantization allows mobile devices to run larger LLMs, but its memory savings do not always translate into faster decoding on mobile NPUs. Their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes, and converting unsupported weight formats on the vector unit can erase the gains from fewer bits. Mixed precision faces an additional constraint: each matrix-unit tile uses one datatype. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations without expanding the weights to wider datatypes during decoding. MixFold then assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with the matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. We compare MixFold with $\mathtt{llama.cpp}$ Hexagon backend on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. Across the Qwen3 model family, MixFold achieves comparable or higher accuracy than $\mathtt{llama.cpp}$'s sub-4-bit formats at matched bits per weight, while decoding 1.16-1.41 times faster and generating 1.5-4.3 times more tokens per joule.

title: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs
abstract: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.

title: Serial Dependence Emerges from Optimizing Vision for Noise Robustness
abstract: Human visual perception is dynamically shaped by the recent past, a phenomenon known as serial dependence. Mechanistic models show that a residual memory trace can generate this dependency, yet its functional purpose (why the visual system should carry information forward in time at all) remains debated. We tested the hypothesis that serial dependence emerges as a normative consequence of optimizing vision for robustness against sensory noise. We trained recurrent autoencoders (a CNN encoder, a ConvGRU memory module, and a CNN decoder) to reconstruct natural videos corrupted by Gaussian noise, with no objective referring to perceptual history. Models that used their temporal memory achieved lower reconstruction error than memory-free counterparts, and this advantage widened as training noise increased, indicating that integrating past context is an adaptive denoising strategy. Probing the trained models with Gabor and dot sequences, we found that memory gave rise to serial dependence spontaneously: an attractive bias toward previous orientations and a spatial "continuity field" toward recently seen locations, both strengthening with training noise. Across temporal delays, the model's serial dependence was strongest for the immediately preceding stimulus and decayed monotonically. This profile quantitatively matched human orientation judgments, including an independent public dataset, once a known response-autocorrelation confound was controlled: an apparent non-monotonicity in one dataset reflected this measurement artifact rather than a genuine model-human mismatch. These findings suggest that serial dependence need not be an idiosyncratic quirk but can arise as a byproduct of optimizing for noise robustness, offering a normative account of perceptual history-dependence that complements existing mechanistic explanations and links behavior to an underlying computational objective.

title: Acceleration of Sparse and Irregular Workloads through Energy-Efficient Stream Extensions
abstract: The slowdown of Moore's law and Dennard scaling has motivated computer architects to uphold performance scaling through architectural specialization. So far, most efforts have focused on highly regular workloads, which exhibit good data locality, ample reuse, and a data-independent execution flow. As this specialization hits diminishing returns, attention shifts towards sparse and irregular workloads, which are essential to applications like sparse neural networks, multiphysics simulations, and graph analytics. However, they lack the convenient properties of highly regular compute that modern architectures are optimized for, resulting in very low (<10%) functional unit utilization on traditional CPUs and GPUs. The most promising approaches to their general hardware acceleration leverage memory streams, which decouple data movement from execution. In this thesis, we explore energy-efficient hardware stream extensions that significantly accelerate sparse and irregular workloads in general-purpose systems without specializing to specific application domains or compromising on regular-workload performance. We design a flexible, core-coupled stream extension supporting affine and indirect streams as well as intersection and union of sparse tensors. We integrate it into an energy-efficient RISC-V compute cluster, achieving significant performance and energy efficiency benefits on general sparse linear algebra, and further use it to accelerate stencil computations, spiking neural network inference, and model-predictive control. We evaluate it at scale in a 432-core 2.5D RISC-V system fabricated in 12nm FinFET, achieving leading compute utilization and energy efficiency on sparse and irregular workloads while remaining competitive on regular workloads. Finally, we extend chip-level interconnects with end-to-end irregular streams, improving performance, energy efficiency, and bus utilization.

title: Topology-only Local Network Alignment, Part 2. DijSLA: Stochastic Greedy Extension for Cross-Species GO Annotation Prediction
abstract: Sequence similarity has long been a strong signal for protein function prediction, whereas the predictive value of network topology has been difficult to verify. Since a protein's function is largely defined by its interaction partners, and since similar interactions are expected across species, aligning protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks by topology alone should uncover functionally related proteins. Topology-only global network alignment has recently produced high-quality functional predictions, but it has yet to be shown that local regions of topological similarity can do the same. We introduce DijSLA (Dijkstra-inspired Stochastic Local Alignment), the first local network alignment algorithm designed from the ground up to use only topology. We adopt a seed-and-extend strategy: starting from seed pairs of proteins with similar network topology, we expand the alignment in a Dijkstra-inspired manner, following edges out of the aligned set to node pairs with near-maximal similarity. Rather than expanding deterministically, we inject randomness so that we can sample many high-quality alignments, in which node pairs with robust topological similarity "rise above" the noise and reveal functional similarity. Using networks and GO annotations from April 2010, we predict annotations validated against those from April 2020. With Network Alignment Frequency (NAF), a robustness measure that correlates with prediction precision, we make predictions with precision on par with or better than the best sequence-based methods and broadly similar to that of global topological alignment. Compared with existing local aligners, DijSLA produces larger, topologically high-quality alignments, which yield dramatically more predictions with higher validation rates, while using less CPU time and far less memory . Code is available at https://github.com/waynebhayes/BLANT/tree/master/CDijkstra.

title: Joint SLA Admission and Risk Allocation for Cloud Resource Provisioning
abstract: Cloud controllers must reserve enough CPU and memory to meet demand without leaving too much capacity idle. Under a shared service-level agreement (SLA), a shortage of CPU or memory (considered as resource) counts toward the same limit. Dividing the allowed shortage risk between them changes how much extra capacity each need. We study this choice when forecast-error histories are short or correlated over time. Our controller compares different approaches to split the allowed shortage risk between resources. For each split, the controller uses historical forecast errors to determine how much extra capacity to reserve. It checks whether the history is enough to support that split and its consistency across different parts of the history. Among the splits that pass, it chooses the one with the lowest combined cost of shortages and idle capacity. Otherwise, the controller continues serving the workload with a calibrated fallback. In our simulation, we set a joint SLA target of sufficient CPU and memory in at least 95% of time slots and used 192 hours of historical forecast errors to structure the controller. Compared with always using fallback, the controller reduced the time slots allocation with either of the resource shortage by 1.04 percentage points on average. This reduction came with a 0.0091 increase in normalized cost from shortages and idle capacity. In the Bitbrains trace, five nonoverlapping test windows did not provide clear evidence of whether shortages increased or decreased. We also examine how execution delays and adjustment limits affect this trade off.

title: Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting
abstract: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Building on ZhuLong, it enhances the task-level harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, isolated sandbox execution, and static checking, then adds governed cross-task self-evolution. Beyond solving individual tasks, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval. On the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, the full task-level harness, with self-evolution disabled, achieves 92.4% pass@1 and outperforms ZhuLong on all five tested LLM backbones. On a harder instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution from the bare configuration surpasses a human-crafted-experience baseline by 2.5 percentage points (80.0% vs. 77.5% pass@1).

title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress
abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.

title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.

title: Finite propagation speed for evolutionary equations
abstract: We study finite speed of propagation in the framework of evolutionary equations introduced by Rainer Picard in 2009. We establish sufficient conditions on the material law, which is represented by an analytic and bounded operator-valued function, and the unbounded spatial operator that ensure finite speed of propagation of information for solutions. Assuming a linear-in-frequency coercivity bound for spatially local material laws, we prove propagation on backward light cones for weighted $L_2$ solutions without a finite initial time, thus identifying hyperbolic-type evolutionary equations. The characteristic-speed threshold depends on the coercive coefficient and the principal spatial matrices, but not on bounded memory or delay terms or potential positive fractional temporal contributions. We illustrate the result with the scalar wave equation, Maxwell's equations, a fractional model in elasticity, and dual-phase-lag thermoelasticity.

title: Contention-Aware Flexible Execution for Machine Learning Workloads
abstract: Concurrent kernel execution is a ubiquitous paradigm in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) across both training and inference. That said, concurrency causes potential slowdown as concurrent kernels contend for limited GPU resources (cores, caches, memory bandwidth), which are shared between these kernels rather than exclusively available to one, as in isolated execution. This raises an important research question: to what extent does concurrency slow down kernel execution and how can it be mitigated. To answer this question, our work presents two studies. First, we characterize concurrent kernel execution extensively for the first time, to our knowledge. We conduct not just performance analysis of concurrent kernels but also memory behavior under concurrency on state-of-the-art AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs designed for datacenter AI, using the AMD-internal millisecond sampler. Based on the observations, we share insights on the slowdown along two dimensions ( memory vs. compute bound, large vs. small kernels) to inform future optimizations. Second, we put the derived insights to use, aiming to deliver higher performance via targeted, flexible overlap of ML operators. Frameworks today make the simple decision of early-first for concurrent kernels, which is suboptimal. Noticing the opportunity that ML dataflow has inherent flexibility in which operators can be overlapped and how hardware resources can be allocated, we deduce simple heuristics to tune both overlap anchors and resource allocation for concurrent kernels to improve performance. We evaluate our proposed contention-aware flexible execution (termed CAFEML) across a variety of ML scenarios (inference decode, inference prefill, training) and demonstrate a speedup of up to 13% end-to-end with simple scheduling changes and no kernel rewrites.

title: Impact of Edge Software Evolution on Audio Tagging Models: An Empirical Study on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano
abstract: Audio tagging is a fundamental task in machine listening, enabling the automatic identification of acoustic events in applications such as intelligent monitoring, industrial inspection, environmental sensing, and smart environments. As these applications increasingly migrate to edge platforms, deployment-oriented metrics such as latency, energy consumption, and resource utilization become critical alongside predictive performance. However, most existing studies evaluate audio tagging models under a single software environment, overlooking the potential impact of software stack evolution on deployment efficiency. This paper investigates how software ecosystem updates affect the execution characteristics of state-of-the-art audio tagging architectures on edge devices. We evaluate representative convolutional and Transformer-based models, including PANNs (CNN and ResNet variants), AST, and PaSST, on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano platform using two generations of NVIDIA's software ecosystem: JetPack 6.2 and JetPack 7.2. Under identical hardware conditions, we analyze inference latency, energy consumption, CPU/GPU utilization, and memory footprint across multiple inference backends and power modes. The results show that software stack evolution can substantially affect deployment performance. JetPack 7.2 reduces latency and energy consumption by more than 50% for several convolutional architectures when combined with TensorRT, while significantly increasing GPU utilization. In contrast, AST exhibits only marginal gains, whereas PaSST shows intermediate behavior. These findings demonstrate that software evolution is a critical factor in Edge AI evaluation and can alter the relative deployment efficiency of competing architectures. Consequently, software stack versions should be explicitly considered when benchmarking and selecting audio tagging models for embedded deployment.

title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory
abstract: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.

title: A functional Breuer-Major theorem under finite variance, with application to the $R/S$ test for long memory
abstract: The Breuer-Major theorem (Breuer and Major, 1983) states that, for a function $G$ of Hermite rank $m$ such that $\mathbb{E}(G^{2}(X))<\infty$, and a stationary Gaussian sequence whose correlation function $r$ satisfies $\sum_{i}|r(i)|^{m}<\infty$, the finite dimensional distributions of the normalized partial sum process of $G(X_{i})$ converge to those of a Brownian motion. Whether the functional version of this result holds under these sole conditions has remained open for a long time, the tightness being known only under additional moment assumptions. In this paper we prove that the functional central limit theorem holds under finite variance only. More generally, we give a high order expansion of the partial sum process which covers both short and long-range dependence: the long-range dependent components converge to Hermite processes, while the remainder converges to a Brownian motion. As an application, we discuss the question of testing long- memory in observed data using the $R/S$ statistics. We derive the limiting distributions of the classical and modified $R/S$ statistics, prove the consistency of the test and propose a data-driven choice of the truncation parameter. A Monte Carlo study compares the performances of the classical and modified $R/S$ statistics for both short- memory and long- memory sequences.

title: Tracktail: Multi-View 3D Point Tracking without Depth Input
abstract: We introduce Tracktail, a novel architecture designed to efficiently track query points in 3D from multiple calibrated views without any depth input. Our architecture separates the task as a per-camera video encoding of features and a per-query decoder. Notably, camera cross-attention is only performed across queries in the decoder, allowing for efficient inference (7 FPS and less than 4 GB memory for 10 views and 100 query points). We further introduce a per-camera scene scale computed from camera geometry, which allows us to normalize inputs and predictions appropriately across a vast variety of dataset scales. We train on a synthetic Multi-View Kubric dataset as well as a novel Multi-View Point Odyssey benchmark dataset, which consists of synthetic renders of humans and animals across 499 frames. Tracktail achieves state-of-the-art results on the Panoptic Studio, DexYCB, and Multi-View Kubric benchmarks, outperforming methods that rely on estimated depth. Tracktail also demonstrates a strong ability to maintain accurate tracking over longer ranges compared to existing methods. Our code, data, and weights are publicly available: https://ai-hhmi.github.io/tracktail/

title: Harnessing Dephasing for Quantum Reservoir Computing with a Minimum Complexity Architecture: Applications to Nonlinear Time-Series Prediction
abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) exploits quantum dynamics for temporal information processing. Quantum noise affects the reservoir dynamics and can either impair computational performance or serve as a computational resource. However, the role of pure dephasing in Hamiltonian encoding QRC remains unclear. In this work, we propose a minimum complexity QRC model that harnesses pure dephasing in an open uniform XX chain. We show that, under suitable input encoding, pure dephasing can ensure the echo state and fading memory properties even without amplitude damping. Furthermore, in the presence of amplitude damping, the proposed quantum reservoir has distinct stationary states for distinct inputs, and introducing pure dephasing alters these states, thereby affecting the reservoir dynamics. Information processing capacity analysis shows that joint control of the two decoherence mechanisms regulates memory and nonlinearity, providing access to diverse capacity profiles. The proposed QRC achieves promising performance on synthetic benchmarks, while its 6-qubit configuration outperforms all three multi-reservoir echo state network baselines on over half of the real-world prediction tasks. These findings highlight pure dephasing as a computational resource for QRC.

title: MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation
abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.

title: FORTH: Grounding Tactile VLA Execution via Forward-Only Proxy-Control Pairing
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are widely credited with force control, operating on the unverified assumption that proxy loss minimization implies physical force grounding. In this work, we demonstrate that this assumption breaks down at three core deployment levels: frozen visual backbones discard contact geometry, downstream losses mask token-level gradient alignment, and discrete indicators trigger optimization collapse. To address these disconnections, we present FORTH, a forward-only measurement harness and execution framework that explicitly pairs the optimization objective at each level with its physical control observable. FORTH incorporates three grounded pillars: a layer-local, forward-only tactile encoder that preserves spatial contact geometry without backpropagation, a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter enabling activation-space updates, and SlipGuard, a continuous tactile verification gate that fires on incipient slip. On an elasto-plastic structural shell, FORTH's closed-loop gate peaks at 29 times lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp, preventing structural crush where the baseline leaves permanent deformation. Furthermore, FORTH matches state-of-the-art execution performance with a 97.6% average success rate across three evaluated LIBERO suites, while reducing peak activation memory by 7.12 times compared to a backpropagated step on the same backbone. Enhanced perception enables deeper physical intelligence.

title: SparseHPS: A Unified Model for Human Pose and Shape across Depth Cameras and LiDARs
abstract: Recovering 3D human pose and shape from point clouds is central to motion capture, robotics and self-driving vehicles, because depth cameras and LiDARs sense a person directly in metric 3D and work under any lighting. However, current approaches are each tailored to one sensor type: point density differs by more than ten times between devices, public datasets are labeled with incompatible body models, and LiDAR approaches need long input sequences to offset sparse scans. In this work, we present SparseHPS, a novel sensor-agnostic network that recovers SMPL-X pose, shape and global translation from a human point cloud with one set of weights, for single frames and streams alike. Specifically, SparseHPS encodes the cloud with a LitePT backbone over sparse voxels, represents every joint by a learnable query decoded with one common head, localizes the body by voting over voxels, and draws temporal context from a causal memory of tokens from the seven preceding frames. A single model is trained on ten datasets that mix rendered clouds with real depth-camera and LiDAR captures, all converted to one body model. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art results on the SLOPER4D and FreeMotion LiDAR benchmarks, where SparseHPS lowers the root-relative joint error by 22% and 11%, respectively, compared with the strongest prior method, which needs 32 frames. On real Azure Kinect captures of held-out HuMMan subjects, SparseHPS attains a joint error of 34.7 mm. Moreover, the current frame alone already yields the bulk of this accuracy.

title: Cavity-Controlled Hysteresis and Multilevel Molecular Switching in Hybrid Optomechanics
abstract: We investigate cavity-controlled hysteresis and multilevel molecular switching in a hybrid molecular optomechanical system composed of a plasmonic nanocavity, a Fabry-Pérot cavity, and an ensemble of molecular vibrations. Molecular-plasmonic optomechanical interaction together with cavity-plasmon hybridization produce bistability and dynamical hysteresis, leading to a history-dependent optical and molecular response. An analytical treatment of the steady-state equations shows that the auxiliary cavity renormalizes the effective optical linewidth and detuning, while the collective molecular interaction generates an effective nonlinearity. Together, these effects enable control of the hysteretic regime through optical detuning, cavity-plasmon coupling, and molecular ensemble size. Beyond bistability, pulsed excitation generates staircase-like molecular dynamics, with ascending or descending vibrational populations depending on the optical driving configuration. In particular, the FP cavity controls the buildup of vibrational excitation, while simultaneous driving of both optical modes enables stepwise vibrational depletion. These results establish hybrid molecular optomechanical systems as a tunable platform for history-dependent and pulse-driven molecular dynamics, with potential applications in nanoscale memory , multilevel information processing, and optically controlled molecular switching.

title: Generative Bayesian modelling of radio antenna beams An application to the MeerKAT radio telescope
abstract: Accurate primary beam models are essential for high-fidelity calibration and imaging in radio astronomy. Traditional approaches either lack the ability to represent realistic antenna patterns (analytical models) or become computationally prohibitive to interpolate for wide-bandwidth observations (electromagnetic simulations, direct holographic measurements). We develop a generative beam model that represents both the spatial structure and the frequency variations in the primary beam while remaining tractable for integration into calibration and imaging pipelines, achieving superior accuracy compared to existing parametric models and reducing data storage compared to data-based models. We adopt a non-parametric Bayesian framework grounded in information field theory, implemented using the NIFTy library. The model represents the beam as a base pattern subject to frequency-dependent geometric transformations (scaling and shifting). Performance is validated through posterior predictive checks (chi^2/dof ~ 1) and compared against traditional models (Gaussian, Airy disc, JimBeam, Eidos, electromagnetic simulation). We apply the method to holographic data of the array-averaged MeerKAT Stokes I beam in the L band. The model achieves 400:1 data compression while preserving statistical consistency with holographic measurements, and outperforms existing approaches by more than an order of magnitude in mean squared deviation. Zernike decomposition of the base beam, combined with the geometric transformations, enables efficient beam reconstruction at arbitrary spatial resolution. The 150 kB per-antenna footprint enables memory -slim integration into calibration and imaging software at negligible cost, scales favourably to large arrays and wide bandwidths, and can be readily adapted to other radio telescopes.

title: Model the Annotation, Not the Noise: Semantic Annotation-Channel Prompt Learning against Noisy Labels
abstract: Parameter-efficient prompt learning has become a cornerstone for adapting pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), yet it remains highly vulnerable to label noise in few-shot Web and retrieval scenarios. Existing noise robust methods typically rely on hard sample selection or deterministic label correction, which discard valuable semantic ambiguity and overlook how observed annotations are actually generated. To bridge this gap, we reformulate noisy prompt learning through the perspective of data generation, proposing SACP, a Semantic-aware Annotation Channel-based Prompt learning framework. Instead of suppressing noise heuristically, SACP decouples latent clean-label prediction from instance-dependent annotation generation. By integrating frozen VLM semantic priors with lightweight visual residuals, SACP constructs a structured annotation channel optimized via generalized expectation-maximization with soft posteriors. Furthermore, a posterior-aware memory is introduced to preserve label uncertainty during test-time inference. Extensive experiments across different synthetic benchmarks and the real-world noisy Food101N dataset demonstrate that SACP achieves state-of-the-art performance against its counterparts in different label noise patterns, especially under severe asymmetric noise.

title: One Behavior, Out of Order: Deterministic Execution and Parallel Simulation of ROS 2 Applications
abstract: System-level simulation is widely used to validate robotic applications before hardware deployment. However, Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2), a popular middleware for such applications, uses asynchronous publish-subscribe communication, which can make application behavior depend on scheduling and the platform. The behavior can then vary across runs and machines even with the same inputs. This nondeterminism makes faults hard to reproduce and tests unreliable. In this paper, we first give ROS 2 applications a lightweight coordination scheme in which every component, including event-driven ones, reads its inputs and writes its outputs at predefined time instants. By decoupling computation and communication, the scheme makes an application deterministic, that is, it always has one behavior for given inputs. Tests are thus repeatable, but for large applications they still take a long time. To speed up these tests, we then present an out-of-order parallel simulation algorithm. From the predefined read and write instants, it knows before the run which activations of components depend on which. It starts each activation as soon as those it depends on have finished. Finally, we implement the algorithm in a simulator that runs existing ROS 2 applications without any change to them or to ROS 2. We evaluate the simulator on industrial use cases and synthetic graphs. On the industrial use cases, it is up to 2.6 times faster than synchronous parallel simulation and needs an order of magnitude less memory for messages than asynchronous parallel simulation.

title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
abstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
abstract: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory . The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. title: ScaleWorld: High-Resolution World Generation through Shared Prediction and Refinement
abstract: High-resolution generation enables video world models to render fine-grained scene structures and textures, but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. We present ScaleWorld, a causal video model that unifies low-resolution world prediction and high-resolution refinement within a single shared backbone. By refining its own predictions, ScaleWorld produces high-resolution world videos without requiring a separate refinement model. For each video chunk, the shared backbone first completes a low-resolution prediction and then performs one-step high-resolution refinement conditioned on that prediction. To support efficient streaming generation, we maintain separate causal states with a long low-resolution history for prediction and a short high-resolution history for refinement. To address task interference during distillation, we separate specialist optimization from capability consolidation and introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD). This procedure transfers prediction and refinement behaviors from specialized teachers into a shared student through local velocity matching under their respective sampling and history policies. {Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScaleWorld achieves high-quality world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.

title: Variants of Beam Search for DiskANN
abstract: Graph-based data structures such as DiskANN, HNSW, and NSG constitute the state of the art for large-scale approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search. Indyk and Xu introduced the notion of $α$-reachable graphs, which include graphs built by DiskANN's slow-preprocessing construction, and proved that greedy search achieves an approximation factor of $\tfrac{α+1}{α-1}$. Independently, Al-Jazzazi et al. proposed adaptive beam search (ABS) with a relaxation parameter $γ> 0$, showing a $\tfrac{2}γ$ approximation on navigable graphs ($α\approx 1$), where greedy search admits no guarantees. In this work, we unify and generalize these results by proving that ABS with parameter $γ$ on $α$-reachable graphs achieves an approximation of $\tfrac{α+1}{α(γ+1)-1}$ for any metric. Moreover, on sorted $α$-reachable graphs (introduced by Gollapudi et al.) under the $\ell_2$ metric, we obtain the tighter bound $\max\bigl(\tfracα{α(γ+1)-1}, \tfrac{α^{2}+1}{α^{2}(γ+1)-1}\bigr)$. Beyond these theoretical results, we design a beam predictor using features inspired by fine-grained analysis of ABS, trained via a constrained objective that minimizes mean distance computations subject to a target recall. On three 100-million-point benchmarks, using graphs built by DiskANN's practical construction, beam predictor lowers mean query latency on SSD-resident indices at matched recall by up to $29.6\%$ relative to classical beam search (CBS). Relative to ABS, it is faster in $11$ of $15$ settings, by up to $6.5\%$, and at most $1.4\%$ slower in the other $4$; at $95\%$ recall, its advantage over ABS grows from $0.8$--$4.2\%$ for $100$ neighbors to $4.6$--$5.6\%$ for $500$ neighbors. In memory , it needs $1.3$--$23.7\%$ fewer distance computations than CBS and $0.0$--$3.9\%$ fewer than ABS.
